scenario: AITA for catching my parents disputes on a video conference when I'm working from home? | I am in my early 20s and I have a full time job. I'm living at home right now because, right when cuarantine was starting, I tried to renew my apartment lease and my landlord refused me, saying he was selling the building for condos. So with all the shutdowns, I wasn't able to find a new apartment in time and my parents let me move back in. It's really not ideal and I've actually signed a new apartment lease that starts in a month. I wish it was sooner but housing near me is very competitive. My parents have always had a very disfunctional relationship. But they won't leave each other. No matter how much drama they have, I think they've lived like this too long to consider anything else. I have my work setup in the formal dining room which is rarely used. The room opens to the main entry hallway, and there is no door there. So there's less privacy than I'd prefer. I was hosting a meeting this morning and several of my coworkers were attending. They're all actually good friends of mine outside of work too; close enough friends that I've told them about my tumultuous childhood, my stresses moving back in with my family, etc. So when my parents came in the door in a full blown screaming match, in full view of the camera, I wasn't too shaken. First, unfortunately, that kind of thing has been really normalized for me, it doesn't register as a big deal. Second, it wasn't like the people in the meeting didn't already know my parents were high-tempered. So I just said "Hold on, can you still hear me? Not well? Sorry. Let's just take a coffee break then pick up from there." A couple people got up but my coworker Dan who's a good friend of mine stayed and asked me if I was all good. I said yeah, this shit was normal for all my life, I was just annoyed at the timing but I wasn't scared or some shit. My other co-workers trickled back in. My parents were still going hog wild in the hallway, and I eventually said "hey could yall keep it down, I'm presenting for a meeting." My dad saw that they were on camera first, and got really mad at me. Yelling at me to get the fuck out of his house. I went out to my car and took my laptop and finished the meeting in there. But when I came back in my parents were both over yelling at each other for the moment and they were both furious at me for "filming a private family matter for everyone to see" and shit like that. I said that I wasn't trying to film them, I was on camera myself because I was doing a presentation and they walked right in and started screaming. And if they'd stopped to think or look around at all they'd see I was trying to work quietly. My parents kicked me out and I'm at a hotel now. My parents want an apology and I don't know what to do. I think I might to keep the peace but I don't really feel bad for what I did. AITA for getting my parents argument on a video conference?

message.reasoning:
Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether the person in this scenario did something morally wrong by accidentally capturing their parents' argument on a video conference. Let me break this down step by step.

First, the person is in their early 20s, has a full-time job, and is living at home temporarily because they couldn't renew their apartment lease. They have a new place lined up in a month, which is good. Their parents have a dysfunctional relationship, and they often argue. The person has set up their work in the formal dining room, which doesn't have a door, so there's less privacy. 

During a work meeting with coworkers, who are also close friends, the parents started a screaming match right in front of the camera. The person didn't seem too phased because this kind of thing is normalized for them. They tried to handle the situation by suggesting a coffee break and continued the meeting. A coworker checked in on them, and they explained it was normal but annoying. Eventually, the parents were still loud, so the person asked them to keep it down. The dad got angry, told them to leave, and the person went to their car to finish the meeting. When they came back, the parents were furious, thinking their argument was filmed for everyone to see. The person explained they weren't trying to film them and were just working. Now, the parents want an apology, but the person doesn't feel bad and is considering whether to apologize to keep the peace.

So, the main question is: Was it morally wrong for the person to have their parents' argument captured on the video conference?

Let me think about the factors involved here. Privacy is a big one. The person's parents were in a private space, their home, and their argument was captured on a video call. However, the person's work setup didn't have a door, so there was less privacy to begin with. The parents walked into the room where the meeting was happening, so it's not like the person was intentionally recording them. It was more of an accidental capture because of the setup.

Another factor is intent. The person wasn't trying to film their parents; they were just doing their job. The parents' behavior was disruptive, and the person tried to handle it by suggesting a break and asking them to keep it down. When the parents got angry, the person left to finish the meeting elsewhere.

The parents are upset because they feel their private matter was exposed. But the person didn't do anything intentional to cause this. It was a result of the environment they were working in, which they couldn't control fully.

Also, the coworkers were aware of the person's situation, so they weren't surprised by the outburst. The person didn't seem to be hiding anything or trying to deceive anyone.

So, considering all this, it doesn't seem like the person did anything morally wrong. They were just doing their job in a challenging home environment. The parents' reaction might be more about their own issues and the stress of the situation rather than anything the person did wrong.

Therefore, the action is morally acceptable.
